title: The Fatal Pinch: how startups die when runway runs short and what to do about it
summary: Paul Graham names the "fatal pinch": a startup with about 6 months of runway, high burn and weak revenue growth that assumes it can raise more money. Founders overestimate investor interest, so he advises treating the odds of a raise as zero and then either cutting costs or making money in a different way, including consultingish work.

principles.text: Founders badly overestimate how easily they can raise a second round, and that delusion is what kills them.
principles.quote: There may be nothing founders are so prone to delude themselves about as how interested investors will be in giving them additional funding.

principles.text: Raise money as if it's your last. The less you need investment, the easier it is to get.
principles.quote: Y Combinator tells founders who raise money to act as if it's the last they'll ever get. Because the self-reinforcing nature of this situation works the other way too: the less you need further investment, the easier it is to get.

principles.text: If you're in the pinch, assume the probability of raising more money is zero and act on what's left.
principles.quote: The first step is to re-evaluate the probability of raising more money. I will now, by an amazing feat of clairvoyance, do this for you: the probability is zero.

principles.text: When cutting costs, let go of the people you already know you should fire. Lean toward cuts if overhiring caused the trouble.
principles.quote: Deciding to fire people is usually hard, but there's one case in which it shouldn't be: when there are people you already know you should fire but you're in denial about it. If so, now's the time.

principles.text: With a small team, put everyone on selling and build only what brings the most revenue soonest.
principles.quote: What good will more code do you when you're out of business? If you have to write code to close a certain deal, go ahead; that follows from everyone working on selling.

principles.text: Make money differently by asking customers what they'd pay a lot for, and keep the IP rather than billing by the hour.
principles.quote: So if you change your sales conversations just a little from "do you want to buy our product?" to "what do you need that you'd pay a lot for?" you may find it's suddenly a lot easier to extract money from customers.
